candidates.tagline: Ford recalled 102,000 trucks because the speedometer lies — and that's technically legal
candidates.story: Ford issued recall 26C46 on October 6, 2026, covering 102,159 F-Series trucks (2025–2026 F-150 through F-750) because the analog speedometer and tachometer can stick or swing to wrong readings; Ford's own filing admits the trucks meet FMVSS 101 (which governs speedometer placement and labeling) but may not meet the standard's 'full intent' — because the federal regulation does not require passenger-car speedometers to be accurate.
candidates.why_funny: America's best-selling truck, priced up to $90,000+, shipped with a speedometer that can lie to you, and the only reason it's being recalled is that Ford felt bad about the spirit of the law it technically didn't break.
candidates.alt: A 2019 Ford F-250 Super Duty XLT pickup truck in white, parked on a paved surface, showing its large front grille, raised ride height, and dual rear wheels

candidates.tagline: Land Rover's $100K 'go anywhere' SUV recalled because rain gets in the camera
candidates.story: JLR issued NHTSA recall 26V678 in October 2026, covering 93,997 Range Rovers (2022–2026) because the tailgate trim has insufficient drain holes — water pools around the rearview camera, potentially damaging it and leaving drivers with a blank backup screen; the engineering solution is for dealers to drill additional drain holes in the underside of the tailgate and replace any water-damaged cameras.
candidates.why_funny: Land Rover built its entire brand on the premise that its vehicles can ford rivers, traverse mud, and conquer any terrain — and yet 94,000 of them need a warranty visit because the tailgate can't drain a rainstorm away from a camera.
candidates.alt: A 2022 Range Rover P400 in dark blue (Varesine Blue) photographed from the front three-quarter angle, showing the full-size luxury SUV's signature floating roof, slim LED headlights, and flush door handles
